opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that supervised learning is not something that happens in nature. Animals don't learn that way. Nobody's giving a squirrel labeled examples saying, "In this situation, here's the correct action you should have taken." That just doesn't happen. What animals have is experience. They take actions, they see what happens, they get rewards and punishments, and they learn from the consequences of their own behavior.

If you look at a young animal, a baby or a little kitten, it's trying things. It's waving its arms around, it's looking at things, it's exploring. There's no teacher telling it the right answer at each moment. There's a stream of experience, and the learning has to come from that stream. It's trial and error, it's prediction, it's noticing that this follows that. That's reinforcement learning and prediction learning, the temporal-difference kind of learning, not supervised learning.

And I think this matters a great deal, because people sometimes say, "Well, children learn by imitation, so it's like supervised learning." But even imitation, when you look at it carefully, isn't really supervised learning. The child sees the parent doing something, but the child is not being told what its own muscles should do. It has to figure out how to produce something like that from its own experience. The target isn't handed over in the form a supervised learner needs.

So supervised learning is a sort of artificial setup. It's useful, it's a good engineering trick, but it's not the basic thing that minds do. The basic thing is learning from experience: you act, you observe, you predict, and you adjust based on what actually happens. If we want to understand intelligence, and build systems that really learn in the world the way animals do, I think that's where we have to focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, supervised learning is learning from examples of what the right behavior is. Someone tells you, here's the input, and here's the correct output, and you adjust yourself to match. And I'd say that basically doesn't happen in animals. There's no one standing over a squirrel telling it which way it should have turned. Animals don't get labeled examples. What they get is consequences. They try things, and some things work out better than others, and they learn from that.

So the two things that really matter, the two kinds of learning we see in animals, are prediction learning and trial-and-error learning. Prediction learning is what Pavlov was studying. You learn that one thing tends to follow another. That's unsupervised in the sense that nobody has to tell you the answer. The world just shows you what happens next, and you compare it to what you expected. And trial-and-error learning, which is what Thorndike and Skinner were studying, is where you do something and you get a reward or you don't, and you do more of what led to the good outcomes. That's reinforcement learning.

Neither of those is supervised learning. In supervised learning, the training signal tells you what you should have done. In reinforcement learning, the training signal only tells you how well you did. It doesn't tell you what to do instead. That's a much weaker signal, but it's the one that's actually available in the world. And so I think it's a little strange that the field has spent so much effort on supervised learning, which is the kind of learning that animals don't do, and treats reinforcement learning as the odd case. If anything it's the other way around. Reinforcement learning is the basic case, the one that an animal living in the world actually faces, and supervised learning is a special, somewhat artificial situation that we constructed because it was convenient.

astra-6.text:
The big distinction is that an animal isn’t given the correct answer. In supervised learning, you’re given an input and a target output, and you learn to produce that target. An animal acts in the world and experiences consequences. It has to figure out what to do from those consequences, without someone telling it what it should have done.

A reward isn’t a label for the correct action. It tells you something about how things turned out, and perhaps only much later. So you have to explore, and you have to figure out which of your earlier actions deserve credit. That’s the reinforcement learning problem.

Animals also learn a great deal just by observing—learning to predict what will happen next. So I wouldn’t say all animal learning is reinforcement learning. But learning to achieve goals through interaction is central, and that’s what the supervised learning formulation leaves out.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in supervised learning, you're given examples of the right answer. You see an input, somebody tells you what the output should have been, and you adjust your system to produce that output. Animals generally don't have that. They take actions, observe what happens, and have to figure out for themselves which actions lead to good outcomes.

That's the distinction between being told what to do and learning what to do from the consequences. If an animal is hungry, it doesn't get a label saying, “Here is the correct sequence of muscle movements to find food.” It has to try things. And the food may come much later, so it has to learn which earlier decisions contributed to getting it. That's the kind of problem reinforcement learning addresses.

Of course, animals also learn about the world without getting a reward for everything they learn. So I wouldn't say all animal learning is reinforcement learning. But learning to act toward goals, without a teacher providing the correct actions—that's a fundamental part of what animals do.
